description: From the executor-to-editor transcript: the HR playbook applied to agents. The two surviving posts are the accountability half of it - a performance review on a cycle, and a name so failure has somewhere to land. The transcript's unattributed survey figure stays out of both. The structural argument does not need it.

posts.title: The performance review
posts.hook: If an AI agent has a job description, it needs a performance review.
body: Handing work to an agent does not hand over responsibility for the work. It only moves where the responsibility sits, and usually it moves it somewhere less specific.

So review the agent the way you would a direct report, on a cycle, against things you named in advance. How often was it accurate. Was it on time. How often did it escalate when it should have, and how often did it not.
That last one is the number worth watching. Escalation rate is the honest measure of whether the boundary you set is real.
Then put a human supervisor next to it on the org chart, by name.

That part is going to stop being a nice-to-have. When something goes wrong in a report that left the building, 'the system categorised it that way' is not an answer that will hold up much longer, with a regulator, an auditor or a customer.

Nobody has to wait for that to arrive to start. The organizations that will handle it comfortably are the ones that were already running the review, for ordinary management reasons, before anyone required it.

One caution from experience with human reviews: a check that never finds anything quietly becomes a rubber stamp. If your review has not caught anything in three months, the interesting question is whether it is still happening.
posts.close: Is there anything your team relies on today whose output nobody, specifically, reviews?
posts.why_it_lands: Takes an accountability argument that usually arrives as compliance pressure and re-routes it through ordinary management practice the reader already believes in.
posts.risk: The legal expectation is a forecast in the source material, not settled law. Keep the hedge in.

posts.title: Name it, so it can be blamed properly
posts.hook: Give the AI agent a name. Not to make it feel like a colleague. To make it impossible to blame in the abstract.
body: The instinct to push back on this is a healthy one. Naming software feels like a step toward pretending it is a person, and it is not a person.
The reason to do it anyway is accountability.

With no name attached, an error sounds like this: the AI formatted the data that way. Everyone nods. Nobody owns it. The AI becomes an abstract scapegoat that cannot be questioned, corrected or performance-managed, and the failure has nowhere to land.
With a name it sounds like this: the intake agent generated that pull on the fourteenth, and Priya signed off on it.
Now there is a document history, a specific step that failed, and two things to fix rather than a vague sense that the technology let everyone down.
A name turns something invisible into an auditable step in a business process. That is the whole argument. It is a filing decision, not a relationship.

It does come with a cost worth watching for. Once a thing has a name, people start talking about what it wants, and a few of them start apologising to it. Keep the name in the process documentation and out of the anthropomorphising, and it stays useful.
posts.close: When something goes wrong in a report your team produces, can you name every step that touched it?
posts.why_it_lands: Opens by agreeing with the reader's objection, then reframes the practice as accountability rather than personification. Agreeing first is what buys the turn.
posts.risk: Do not open with the recommendation unqualified. The objection has to come in the first two lines or the post loses half its readers.
